claim: Transposable elements (TEs) are repetitive sequences representing ~45% of the human and mouse genomes.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are repetitive sequences representing ~45% of the human and mouse genomes (Treangen and Salzberg, 2011; Deniz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Treangen and Salzberg, 2011; Deniz et al., 2019).

claim: TEs are highly expressed by medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs).
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are repetitive sequences representing ~45% of the human and mouse genomes and are highly expressed by medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs).
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TE expression in the human thymus is high and shows extensive age- and cell lineage-related variations.
source: We report that TE expression in the human thymus is high and shows extensive age- and cell lineage-related variations.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: TE expression correlates with multiple transcription factors in all cell types of the human thymus.
source: TE expression correlates with multiple transcription factors in all cell types of the human thymus.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 2 and related text.

claim: Two cell types express particularly broad TE repertoires: mTECs and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs).
source: Two cell types express particularly broad TE repertoires: mTECs and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs).
evidence: Supported by Shannon entropy analysis in Figure 3a and differential expression analysis in Figure 3d.

claim: TEs interact with transcription factors essential for mTEC development and function (e.g., PAX1 and REL).
source: In mTECs, transcriptomic data suggest that TEs interact with transcription factors essential for mTEC development and function (e.g., PAX1 and REL)
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic correlation analysis and TF binding motif analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: TEs generate MHC-I-associated peptides implicated in thymocyte education.
source: immunopeptidomic data showed that TEs generate MHC-I-associated peptides implicated in thymocyte education.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 6.

claim: AIRE, FEZF2, and CHD4 regulate small yet non-redundant sets of TEs in murine mTECs.
source: Notably, AIRE, FEZF2, and CHD4 regulate small yet non-redundant sets of TEs in murine mTECs.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data from knockout mice presented in Figure 5.

claim: Human thymic pDCs homogenously express large numbers of TEs that likely form dsRNA.
source: Human thymic pDCs homogenously express large numbers of TEs that likely form dsRNA, which can activate innate immune receptors
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data (Figure 4a) and immunostaining showing dsRNA in pDCs (Figure 4c-d).

claim: TEs in thymic pDCs can activate innate immune receptors, potentially explaining why thymic pDCs constitutively secrete IFN ɑ/β.
source: which can activate innate immune receptors, potentially explaining why thymic pDCs constitutively secrete IFN ɑ/β.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the presence of dsRNA and gene set enrichment analysis (Figure 4e).

claim: Orchestrating TE expression in thymic cells is critical to prevent autoimmunity in vertebrates.
source: Therefore, we propose that orchestrating TE expression in thymic cells is critical to prevent autoimmunity in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: The thymus is the only site where T lymphocytes can be properly educated to distinguish self from non-self in jawed vertebrates.
source: In jawed vertebrates, the thymus is the only site where T lymphocytes can be properly educated to distinguish self from non-self (Boehm and Swann, 2014; Suo et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Oncostatin M-transgenic mice where T-cell production occurs exclusively in the lymph nodes present severe autoimmunity and cannot fight infections.
source: This is vividly illustrated by Oncostatin M-transgenic mice, where T-cell production occurs exclusively in the lymph nodes (Terra et al., 2005). These mice harbor normal numbers of T-cell receptors (TCRs) αβ T cells but present severe autoimmunity and cannot fight infections (Blais et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Intrathymic generation of a functional T-cell repertoire depends on choreographed interactions between the TCRs of thymocytes and peptides presented by MHC molecules on various antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
source: Intrathymic generation of a functional T-cell repertoire depends on choreographed interactions between the TCRs of thymocytes and peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules on various antigen-presenting cells (APCs) (Zuñiga-Pflucker et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge in immunology.

claim: Positive selection depends on self-antigens presented by cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) and ensures that TCRs recognize antigens in the context of the host's MHC molecules.
source: Positive selection depends on self-antigens presented by cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) and ensures that TCRs recognize antigens in the context of the host's MHC molecules (Breed et al., 2018; Dervović and Zúñiga-Pflücker, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: The establishment of central tolerance depends on two main classes of APCs located in the thymic medulla: dendritic cells (DCs) and medullary TEC (mTEC).
source: The establishment of central tolerance depends on two main classes of APCs located in the thymic medulla: dendritic cells (DCs) and medullary TEC (mTEC) (Lebel et al., 2020; Srinivasan et al., 2021; Cheng and Anderson, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Thymic fibroblasts and B cells have a more limited contribution to central tolerance compared to DCs and mTECs.
source: Two other APC types have a more limited contribution to central tolerance: thymic fibroblasts and B cells (Perera et al., 2016; Nitta et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High avidity interactions between thymic APCs and autoreactive thymocytes lead to thymocyte deletion (negative selection) or generation of regulatory T cells (Treg).
source: High avidity interactions between thymic APCs and autoreactive thymocytes lead to thymocyte deletion (negative selection) or generation of regulatory T cells (Treg) (Malhotra et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Recent single-cell RNA-seq studies have identified several subpopulations of mTECs including immature mTEC(I), mTEC(II), fully differentiated corneocyte-like mTEC(III), and mimetic mTECs.
source: Indeed, recent single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) studies have identified several subpopulations of mTECs: immature mTEC(I) that stimulate thymocyte migration to the medulla via chemokine secretion (Lkhagvasuren et al., 2013), mTEC(II) that express high levels of MHC and are essential to tolerance induction, fully differentiated corneocyte-like mTEC(III) that foster a pro-inflammatory microenvironment (Laan et al., 2021), and finally mimetic mTECs that express peripheral tissue antigens (Michelson et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published scRNA-seq studies.

claim: AIRE, FEZF2, and CHD4 drive the expression of non-redundant sets of peripheral tissue antigens in mTECs.
source: Three different proteins whose loss of function leads to severe autoimmunity, AIRE, FEZF2, and CHD4, have been shown to drive the expression of non-redundant sets of peripheral tissue antigens in mTECs (Ramsey et al., 2002; Takaba et al., 2015; Tomofuji et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DCs are separated into three main populations: conventional DC 1 and 2 (cDC1 and cDC2) and plasmacytoid DC (pDC).
source: DCs, on the other hand, are separated into three main populations. Conventional DC 1 and 2 (cDC1 and cDC2) have an unmatched ability to present both endogenous antigens and exogenous antigens acquired via cross-presentation or cross-dressing (Ginhoux et al., 2022). Plasmacytoid DC (pDC) are less effective APCs than cDCs, their primary role being to produce interferon alpha (IFNɑ) (Ginhoux et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Thymic pDCs originate from intrathymic IRF8hi precursors.
source: Notably, thymic pDCs originate from intrathymic IRF8hi precursors, and, in contrast to extrathymic pDCs, they constitutively secrete high amounts of IFNɑ (Colantonio et al., 2011; Lavaert et al., 2020; Le et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Thymic pDCs constitutively secrete high amounts of IFNɑ, in contrast to extrathymic pDCs.
source: Notably, thymic pDCs originate from intrathymic IRF8hi precursors, and, in contrast to extrathymic pDCs, they constitutively secrete high amounts of IFNɑ (Colantonio et al., 2011; Lavaert et al., 2020; Le et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Constitutive IFNɑ secretion by thymic pDCs regulates the late stages of thymocyte development by promoting the generation of Tregs and innate CD8 T cells.
source: This constitutive IFNɑ secretion by thymic pDCs regulates the late stages of thymocyte development by promoting the generation of Tregs and innate CD8 T cells (Xing et al., 2016; Hanabuchi et al., 2010; Martín Gayo et al., 2010; Martinet et al., 2015; Epeldegui et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most TEs can be grouped into three categories: the long and short interspersed nuclear elements (LINE and SINE, respectively) and the long terminal repeats (LTRs).
source: Most TEs can be grouped into three categories: the long and short interspersed nuclear elements (LINE and SINE, respectively) and the long terminal repeats (LTRs).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about TE classification.

claim: TE categories are subdivided into over 800 subfamilies based on sequence homology.
source: These broad categories are subdivided into over 800 subfamilies based on sequence homology (Bourque et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: TE expression is typically repressed in host cells to prevent deleterious integrations of TE sequences in protein-coding genes.
source: TE expression is typically repressed in host cells to prevent deleterious integrations of TE sequences in protein-coding genes (Argueso et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: TEs are expressed at higher levels in human mTECs than in any other MHC-expressing tissues and organs (excluding the testis).
source: Unexpectedly, TEs were recently found to be expressed at higher levels in human mTECs than in any other MHC-expressing tissues and organs (i.e., excluding the testis) (Larouche et al., 2020; Carter et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some TEs are translated and generate MHC I-associated peptides (MAP).
source: Since some TEs are translated and generate MHC I-associated peptides (MAP) (Larouche et al., 2020), they might induce TE-specific central tolerance (Kassiotis, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TEs provide binding sites to transcription factors.
source: Additionally, TEs provide binding sites to transcription factors (TFs) and stimulate cytokine secretion via the formation of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) (Chuong et al., 2016; Bogdan et al., 2020; Adoue et al., 2019; Lefkopoulos et al., 2020; Lima-Junior et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TEs stimulate cytokine secretion via the formation of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA).
source: Additionally, TEs provide binding sites to transcription factors (TFs) and stimulate cytokine secretion via the formation of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) (Chuong et al., 2016; Bogdan et al., 2020; Adoue et al., 2019; Lefkopoulos et al., 2020; Lima-Junior et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering revealed three clusters of TE subfamilies based on their pattern of expression during thymic development.
source: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering revealed three clusters of TE subfamilies based on their pattern of expression during thymic development (Figure 1b, upper panel)
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: LINE and SINE subfamilies were enriched in cluster 1 (maximal expression at early embryonic stages persisting throughout ontogeny).
source: LINE and SINE subfamilies were enriched in cluster 1, whereas LTR subfamilies were significantly enriched in clusters 2 and 3 (Figure 1b, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: LTR subfamilies were significantly enriched in clusters 2 and 3.
source: LINE and SINE subfamilies were enriched in cluster 1, whereas LTR subfamilies were significantly enriched in clusters 2 and 3 (Figure 1b, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Expression of individual LINE and SINE subfamilies was highly shared among different cell types.
source: Expression of individual LINE and SINE subfamilies was highly shared among different cell types (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The LTR subfamilies' expression pattern was shared by fewer cell subsets and adopted a quasi-random distribution.
source: In contrast, the LTR subfamilies' expression pattern was shared by fewer cell subsets and adopted a quasi-random distribution (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Cell cycling scores negatively correlated with TE expression in various thymic cell subsets, particularly for LINE and SINE subfamilies shared among cell types.
source: Cell cycling scores negatively correlated with TE expression in various thymic cell subsets, particularly for LINE and SINE subfamilies shared among cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: ZNF10 is a probable repressor of L1 subfamilies in Th17 and NK cells.
source: whereas analysis of KZFP expression identified ZNF10 as a probable repressor of L1 subfamilies in Th17 and NK cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: TF-TE interactions were observed in all thymic cell populations.
source: TF-TE interactions were observed in all thymic cell populations (Figure 2c and d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by network analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The number of interactions and the complexity of the interaction networks were much higher in mTECs than in other cell populations.
source: However, the number of interactions and the complexity of the interaction networks were much higher in mTECs than in other cell populations (Figure 2c and d, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by network analysis shown in Figure 2c, d and supplements.

claim: Several TFs instrumental in thymus development and thymopoiesis interacted with TE subfamilies, including NFKB1, REL, and PAX1 in mTECs.
source: Several TFs instrumental in thymus development and thymopoiesis interacted with TE subfamilies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1d). These TFs include the NFKB1 and REL subunits of the NF-κB complex and PAX1 in mTECs (Baik et al., 2016; Akiyama et al., 2008; Yamazaki et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by network analysis and citations to literature on TF function.

claim: JUND interacts with TE subfamilies in thymocytes.
source: and JUND in thymocytes (Meixner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by network analysis and citation to literature on TF function.

claim: In DCs, the most notable TF-TE interactions involved interferon regulatory factors (IRF) and TCF4.
source: In DCs, the most notable TF-TE interactions involved interferon regulatory factors (IRF), which regulate the late stages of T-cell maturation, and TCF4, which is essential for pDC development (Xing et al., 2016; Cisse et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by network analysis and citations to literature on TF function.

claim: Significant interactions between CTCF and TE subfamilies were found in mTECs and endothelial cells.
source: Finally, we found significant interactions between CTCF and TE subfamilies in mTECs and endothelial cells, suggesting that the binding of CTCF to TE sequences affects the tridimensional structure of the chromatin in the thymic stroma (Choudhary et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by network analysis and inference based on known CTCF function.

claim: LINE and SINE subfamilies that occupy more genomic space interacted with higher numbers of transcription factors.
source: Interestingly, LINE and SINE subfamilies that occupy more genomic space interacted with higher numbers of transcription factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Several TE promoter and enhancer candidates were found in all eight hematopoietic cell types analyzed, with a striking overrepresentation of LINE and SINE compared to LTR sequences.
source: We found several TE promoter and enhancer candidates in all eight hematopoietic cell types analyzed, with a striking overrepresentation of LINE and SINE compared to LTR sequences (Figure 2f and Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by analysis of histone marks from ENCODE data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: 19% of ETS1 peaks overlap with TE sequences.
source: Indeed, 19% of ETS1 peaks overlap with TE sequences (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 2g.

claim: ETS1 peaks overlapped with TE sequences in the promoter regions of PRF1 and KLRD1, two genes critical for NK cells' effector functions.
source: Notably, ETS1 peaks overlapped with TE sequences (Figure 2h, in red) in the promoter regions of PRF1 and KLRD1, two genes critical for NK cells' effector functions (Kim et al., 2014; Gunturi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 2h and citations to literature on gene function.

claim: The diversity of TEs expressed in the T-cell lineage decreases during differentiation according to the hierarchy: DN thymocytes > DP thymocytes > SP thymocytes.
source: First, the diversity of TEs expressed in the T-cell lineage decreases during differentiation according to the following hierarchy: DN thymocytes > DP thymocytes > SP thymocytes (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Shannon entropy analysis shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among thymic APCs implicated in positive and negative selection, cTECs, mTECs, and DCs expressed broader repertoires of TEs than B cells and fibroblasts.
source: Second, among the populations of thymic APCs implicated in positive and negative selection (Figure 3a, orange dots), cTECs, mTECs, and DCs expressed broader repertoires of TEs than B cells and fibroblasts.
evidence: Supported by Shannon entropy analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: cTECs and DCs expressed highly diverse TE repertoires at both the population and individual cell levels.
source: While cTECs and DCs expressed highly diverse TE repertoires at both the population and individual cell levels, the breadth of TE expression in mTECs was found only at the population level (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by Shannon entropy analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The breadth of TE expression in mTECs was found only at the population level, not at the individual cell level.
source: While cTECs and DCs expressed highly diverse TE repertoires at both the population and individual cell levels, the breadth of TE expression in mTECs was found only at the population level (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by Shannon entropy analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Intercellular heterogeneity was higher for mTECs than other cell populations.
source: Accordingly, intercellular heterogeneity (i.e., deviation from the linear model) was higher for mTECs than other cell populations (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by deviation analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: 32.01% of TE subfamilies were overexpressed in pDCs.
source: pDCs and mTEC(II) overexpressed a broader TE repertoire than other APCs: 32.01% of subfamilies were overexpressed in pDCs and 10.88% in mTEC(II) (Figure 3d and Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: 10.88% of TE subfamilies were overexpressed in mTEC(II).
source: pDCs and mTEC(II) overexpressed a broader TE repertoire than other APCs: 32.01% of subfamilies were overexpressed in pDCs and 10.88% in mTEC(II) (Figure 3d and Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: pDCs overexpressed LTRs, LINEs, and SINEs, including several Alu and L1 subfamilies.
source: Indeed, pDCs overexpressed LTRs, LINEs, and SINEs, including several Alu and L1 subfamilies (Figure 3d and Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Other thymic APCs predominantly overexpressed LTRs.
source: In contrast, other thymic APCs predominantly overexpressed LTRs.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Most TE subfamilies were expressed by <25% of cells of the mTEC(II) population.
source: Indeed, whereas most TE subfamilies were expressed by <25% of cells of the mTEC(II) population, an important proportion of TEs were expressed by >75% of pDCs (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by frequency of expression analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: An important proportion of TEs were expressed by >75% of pDCs.
source: Indeed, whereas most TE subfamilies were expressed by <25% of cells of the mTEC(II) population, an important proportion of TEs were expressed by >75% of pDCs (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by frequency of expression analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Overexpression of TE subfamilies was shared between pDC metacells but not mTEC(II) metacells.
source: This analysis revealed that overexpression of TE subfamilies was shared between pDC metacells but not mTEC(II) metacells, reinforcing the idea that TE expression adopts a mosaic pattern in the mTEC(II) population (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by metacell analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Extrathymic pDCs express TE sequences at similar or lower levels than other splenic cells.
source: This revealed that extrathymic pDCs express TE sequences at similar or lower levels than other splenic cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by analysis of splenic scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TE expression was globally higher in thymic than in extrathymic pDCs.
source: This analysis confirmed that TE expression was globally higher in thymic than in extrathymic pDCs (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The intensity of the J2 signal (dsRNA staining) was more than tenfold higher in CD123+ cells (pDCs) relative to CD123- cells.
source: The intensity of the J2 signal was more than tenfold higher in CD123+ relative to CD123- cells (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: Thymic pDCs contain large amounts of dsRNAs.
source: We conclude that thymic pDCs contain large amounts of dsRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from J2 antibody staining data shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: The percentage of reads from mitochondrial genes was typically lower in pDCs than in other thymic APCs.
source: Strikingly, whereas the percentage of reads from mitochondrial genes was typically lower in pDCs than in other thymic APCs, the proportion of the transcriptome originating from TEs was higher in pDCs (~22%) by several orders of magnitude (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome composition analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The proportion of the transcriptome originating from TEs was higher in pDCs (~22%) by several orders of magnitude compared to other thymic APCs.
source: Strikingly, whereas the percentage of reads from mitochondrial genes was typically lower in pDCs than in other thymic APCs, the proportion of the transcriptome originating from TEs was higher in pDCs (~22%) by several orders of magnitude (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome composition analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Thymic pDCs harbored moderate yet significant enrichment of gene signatures of RIG-I and MDA5-mediated IFN ɑ/β signaling compared to all other thymic APCs.
source: Notably, thymic pDCs harbored moderate yet significant enrichment of gene signatures of RIG-I and MDA5-mediated IFN ɑ/β signaling compared to all other thymic APCs (Figure 4e and Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: mTEC(II) express AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2.
source: First, we validated that mTEC(II) express AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 in the human scRNA-seq dataset (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 regulate TE sequences in murine mTECs, but the magnitude and directionality of this regulation differed.
source: Differential expression analyses between knock-out (KO) and wild-type (WT) mice showed that these three factors regulate TE sequences, but the magnitude and directionality of this regulation differed (Figure 5b and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: CHD4 had the biggest impact on TE expression by inducing 433 TE loci and repressing 463.
source: Indeed, while CHD4 had the biggest impact on TE expression by inducing 433 TE loci and repressing 463, FEZF2's impact was minimal, with 97 TE loci induced and 60 repressed (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: FEZF2's impact on TE expression was minimal, with 97 TE loci induced and 60 repressed.
source: Indeed, while CHD4 had the biggest impact on TE expression by inducing 433 TE loci and repressing 463, FEZF2's impact was minimal, with 97 TE loci induced and 60 repressed (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: AIRE mainly acted as a repressor of TE sequences, with 326 loci repressed and 171 induced.
source: Besides, AIRE mainly acted as a repressor of TE sequences, with 326 loci repressed and 171 induced (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: There was minimal overlap between the TE sequences regulated by AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2.
source: Interestingly, there was minimal overlap between the TE sequences regulated by AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2, indicating that they have non-redundant roles in TE regulation (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 preferentially targeted LTR and LINE elements.
source: Additionally, AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 preferentially targeted LTR and LINE elements, with significant enrichment of specific subfamilies such as MTA_Mm-int and RLTR4_Mm that are induced by Aire and Fezf2, respectively (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: AIRE and CHD4 preferentially targeted evolutionary young TE sequences.
source: While AIRE and CHD4 preferentially targeted evolutionary young TE sequences, the age of the TE sequence did not seem to affect the regulation by FEZF2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by age analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The age of the TE sequence did not seem to affect the regulation by FEZF2.
source: While AIRE and CHD4 preferentially targeted evolutionary young TE sequences, the age of the TE sequence did not seem to affect the regulation by FEZF2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by age analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The distance between regulated TE loci was smaller than the distributions of randomly selected TEs.
source: We also noticed that the distance between regulated TE loci was smaller than the distributions of randomly selected TEs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 nonrandomly affect the expression of TE sequences located in specific genomic regions.
source: This suggests that AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 nonrandomly affect the expression of TE sequences located in specific genomic regions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that distance between regulated TEs is smaller than random.

claim: Most TE loci targeted by AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 were located in intronic and intergenic regions.
source: We observed no significant differences in the genomic localization of TE loci targeted by AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 relative to the genomic localization of all TE sequences in the murine genome: most TE loci were located in intronic and intergenic regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by genomic localization analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The intron retention ratio was similar for TEs regulated or not by AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2.
source: Enrichment for intronic TEs could not be ascribed to induction of global intron retention: the intron retention ratio was similar for TEs regulated or not by AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by intron retention analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e.

claim: TE loci induced by AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 were all marked by H3K4me3.
source: ChIP-seq-based analysis of permissive histone marks showed that TE loci induced by AIRE, CHD4, and FEZF2 were all marked by H3K4me3 (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: 31.42% of AIRE peaks overlap with TE sequences.
source: As a proof of concept, we validated that 31.42% of AIRE peaks overlap with TE sequences by reanalyzing ChIP-seq data, confirming AIRE's potential to bind TE sequences (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Four TE-derived MAPs were identified in mTECs and two in cTECs.
source: MS analyses enabled the identification of a total of 1636 and 1714 MAPs in mTECs and cTECs, respectively. From these, we identified four TE-derived MAPs in mTECs and two in cTECs, demonstrating that TEs can be translated and presented by MHC I in the thymic cortex and medulla (Figure 6b and Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: TE-derived MAPs were coded by the three major groups of TE: LINEs (n = 1), LTRs (n = 1), and SINEs (n = 4).
source: These MAPs were coded by the three major groups of TE: LINEs (n = 1), LTRs (n = 1), and SINEs (n = 4).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: TECs highly and ubiquitously expressed the MAP-generating TE subfamilies.
source: Strikingly, TECs highly and ubiquitously expressed the MAP-generating TE subfamilies.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The contribution of TEs to the MAP repertoire of cTECs and mTECs might be significantly underestimated by the limits of detection of MS.
source: These results suggest that the contribution of TEs to the MAP repertoire of cTECs and mTECs might be significantly underestimated by the limits of detection of MS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high expression of TE subfamilies that generate MAPs.

claim: TEs can generate MAPs presented by cTECs and mTECs, which can contribute to thymocyte education.
source: Nonetheless, our data provide direct evidence that TEs can generate MAPs presented by cTECs and mTECs, which can contribute to thymocyte education.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 6.

claim: TEs encode proteins and noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression at multiple levels.
source: Mechanistically, TEs encode proteins and noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression at multiple levels (Bourque et al., 2018; Frank and Feschotte, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Regulation of IFN signaling and triggering innate sensors are the best-characterized roles of TEs in the mammalian immune system.
source: Regulation of IFN signaling and triggering innate sensors are the best-characterized roles of TEs in the mammalian immune system (Kassiotis, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: TEs are immunogenic and can elicit adaptive immune responses implicated in autoimmune diseases.
source: TEs are immunogenic and can elicit adaptive immune responses implicated in autoimmune diseases (Larouche et al., 2020; Kassiotis, 2023; Gröger and Cynis, 2018; Volkman and Stetson, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The negative correlation between TE expression and cell cycle scores in the thymus is coherent with recent data showing that transcriptional activity of L1s is increased in senescent cells.
source: The negative correlation between TE expression and cell cycle scores in the thymus is coherent with recent data showing that transcriptional activity of L1s is increased in senescent cells (De Cecco et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study's findings to published literature.

claim: PAX1 is essential for the development of TEC progenitors.
source: PAX1 is essential for the development of TEC progenitors (Yamazaki et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RELB is essential for the development and differentiation of mTECs.
source: and RELB is for the development and differentiation of mTECs (Mouri et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RelB-deficient mice have reduced thymic cellularity, markedly fewer mTECs, lack Aire expression, and suffer from autoimmunity.
source: RelB-deficient mice have reduced thymic cellularity, markedly fewer mTECs, lack Aire expression, and suffer from autoimmunity (Akiyama et al., 2008; O'Sullivan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Under the influence of Aire, Fezf2, and Chd4, mTECs collectively express almost the entire exome.
source: Under the influence of Aire, Fezf2, and Chd4, mTECs collectively express almost the entire exome (Sansom et al., 2014; Pierre et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Promiscuous expression of tissue-restricted genes in mTECs adopts a mosaic pattern: individual tissue-restricted genes are expressed in a small fraction of mTECs.
source: Hence, promiscuous expression of tissue-restricted genes in mTECs adopts a mosaic pattern: individual tissue-restricted genes are expressed in a small fraction of mTECs (Michelson et al., 2022; Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: mTECs express an extensive repertoire of TEs in a mosaic pattern (i.e., with considerable intercellular heterogeneity).
source: The present work shows that mTECs also express an extensive repertoire of TEs in a mosaic pattern (i.e., with considerable intercellular heterogeneity).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: TCRs interact with MAPs, not transcripts.
source: However, (i) TCRs interact with MAPs, not transcripts
evidence: This represents established knowledge in immunology.

claim: The MAP repertoire cannot be inferred from the transcriptome.
source: and (ii) the MAP repertoire cannot be inferred from the transcriptome (Shapiro and Bassani-Sternberg, 2023; Caron et al., 2011; Admon, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: K5D1 mice present prominent thymic hyperplasia.
source: Using K5D1 mice presenting prominent thymic hyperplasia, we conducted MS searches of TE MAPs
evidence: This is a known characteristic of K5D1 mice cited in the manuscript.

claim: TE MAPs have been detected in normal and neoplastic extrathymic cells.
source: As TE MAPs have been detected in normal and neoplastic extrathymic cells (Larouche et al., 2020; Laumont et al., 2018; Burbage et al., 2023; Shah et al., 2023), the presentation of TEs by mTECs is likely essential to central tolerance.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The presentation of TEs by mTECs is likely essential to central tolerance.
source: As TE MAPs have been detected in normal and neoplastic extrathymic cells (Larouche et al., 2020; Laumont et al., 2018; Burbage et al., 2023; Shah et al., 2023), the presentation of TEs by mTECs is likely essential to central tolerance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of TE MAPs in various cell types.

claim: Immunopeptidomic studies should not be limited to protein-coding genes (2% of the genome) but also encompass non-coding sequences such as TEs.
source: In line with vibrant plaidoyers for a collaborative Human Immunopeptidome Project (Vizcaíno et al., 2020; Shao et al., 2018), our work suggests that immunopeptidomic studies should not be limited to protein-coding genes (2% of the genome) but also encompass non-coding sequences such as TEs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Thymic and extrathymic pDCs develop independently from each other from different precursor cells.
source: They develop independently from each other from different precursor cells (Lavaert et al., 2020; Le et al., 2020; Weijer et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IFN ɑ/β secretion is inducible in extrathymic pDCs but constitutive in thymic pDCs.
source: IFN ɑ/β secretion is inducible in extrathymic pDCs but constitutive in thymic pDCs (Ginhoux et al., 2022; Colantonio et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The constitutive IFN ɑ/β secretion by thymic pDCs is instrumental in the terminal differentiation of thymocytes and the generation of Tregs and innate CD8 T cells.
source: In line with the location of pDCs in the thymic medulla, their constitutive IFN ɑ/β secretion is instrumental in the terminal differentiation of thymocytes and the generation of Tregs and innate CD8 T cells (Xing et al., 2016; Hanabuchi et al., 2010; Martín Gayo et al., 2010; Martinet et al., 2015; Epeldegui et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High TE expression is a feature of thymic, but not extrathymic, pDCs.
source: We report here that high TE expression is also a feature of thymic, but not extrathymic, pDCs.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of thymic and splenic pDCs shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Recognition of TE-derived dsRNAs by innate immune receptors promotes a pro-inflammatory environment favorable to the establishment of central tolerance in the thymic medulla.
source: As such, our data suggest that recognition of TE-derived dsRNAs by innate immune receptors promotes a pro-inflammatory environment favorable to the establishment of central tolerance in the thymic medulla.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the study's findings.

claim: The integration of genetic parasites such as TEs is a source of genetic conflicts with the host.
source: It should be reminded that the integration of genetic parasites such as TEs is a source of genetic conflicts with the host.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: The emergence of adaptive immunity gave rise to higher-order conflicts between TEs and their vertebrate hosts.
source: Notably, the emergence of adaptive immunity gave rise to higher-order conflicts between TEs and their vertebrate hosts (Kassiotis, 2023; Boehm et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The thymus is the central battlefield for conflict resolution between TEs and T cells in vertebrates.
source: Our data suggest that the thymus is the central battlefield for conflict resolution between TEs and T cells in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the study's findings.

claim: More than 90% of putative causal variants associated with autoimmune diseases are in allegedly noncoding regions of the genome.
source: Consistent with the implication of TEs in autoimmunity, more than 90% of putative causal variants associated with autoimmune diseases are in allegedly noncoding regions of the genome (Harroud and Hafler, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Autoimmune diseases affect up to 10% of humans.
source: The crucial challenge for the immune system is developing immune tolerance towards TEs to prevent autoimmune diseases that affect up to 10% of humans (Harroud and Hafler, 2023)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Numerous TF-TE interactions were conserved between hematolymphoid and stromal cell subsets.
source: Numerous TF-TE interactions were conserved between hematolymphoid and stromal cell subsets (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by sharing analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The expression of 809 TE subfamilies was quantified in the scRNA-seq dataset of human thymi.
source: To do so, we quantified the expression of 809 TE subfamilies (classified according to the RepeatMasker annotations) in the scRNA-seq dataset of human thymi created by Park et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Cells were clustered in 19 populations representing the main constituents of the thymic hematolymphoid and stromal compartments.
source: Cells were clustered in 19 populations representing the main constituents of the thymic hematolymphoid and stromal compartments (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology and results shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The expression of TE subfamilies was quantified at all developmental stages available, ranging from 7 post-conception weeks (pcw) to 40 years of age.
source: The expression of TE subfamilies was quantified at all developmental stages available, ranging from 7 post-conception weeks (pcw) to 40 years of age (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.
